title: Tangents to a Circle: Secant vs Tangent Limits & Theorem 10.1 Perpendicularity Proof
description: Understand the geometric definition of a tangent to a circle as a limiting case of a secant when the two intersection points coincide. Rigorously prove Theorem 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact, using the shortest distance property.
key_concepts: Secant: A straight line that intersects a circle in two distinct points
Tangent: A straight line that touches the circle at exactly one point (Point of Contact)
Limiting Case: A tangent is the limiting position of a secant when its two end-points of intersection coincide
Theorem 10.1: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact

Shortest Distance Principle: The shortest distance from an external point to a straight line is the perpendicular distance; any point Q on the tangent line other than P lies strictly outside the circle, hence OQ > OP
subtopics: Differentiating non-intersecting lines, secants, and tangents
Full formal proof of Theorem 10.1 by contradiction / shortest distance
Number of tangents from points inside, on, and outside a circle

worked_examples.given: A circle C(O, r) with centre O and a tangent line XY touching the circle at point P. OP is the radius through the point of contact P.
worked_examples.formula: The shortest distance between a given point and a given straight line is the perpendicular distance.
worked_examples.substitution: Take any point Q on XY distinct from P. Segment OQ intersects the circle at R. Since R lies on circle, OR = OP. Therefore OQ = OR + RQ = OP + RQ > OP.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Point P lies on the circle and on the line XY.
2. Since XY is tangent, P is the UNIQUE point of intersection with the circle.
3. Every other point Q on line XY lies strictly outside the circle.
4. Therefore, distance OQ > OP (radius) for every point Q ≠ P on XY.
5. OP is the shortest distance from centre O to line XY.
6. Since the shortest distance is perpendicular, OP ⊥ XY.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: OP ⊥ XY (The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact)
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
A circle C(O, r) with centre O and a tangent XY touching the circle at point P. OP is the radius through the point of contact P.

TO PROVE:
OP ⊥ XY.

CONSTRUCTION:
Take any point Q on the tangent line XY other than P. Join OQ. Let OQ intersect the circle at point R.

PROOF:
Step 1: Position of Q relative to the circle:
Since XY is a tangent to the circle at point P, P is the only point on the line XY that lies on the circle.
Every other point on the line XY must lie strictly outside the circle.
Therefore, point Q lies outside the circle.

Step 2: Compare lengths OQ and OP:
Since point R lies on the circle and between O and Q:
OQ = OR + RQ
Since OR = OP (radii of the same circle):
OQ = OP + RQ
Since RQ > 0:
OQ > OP.

Step 3: Conclude shortest distance:
This inequality OQ > OP holds true for EVERY point Q on the line XY, except the point of contact P.
Therefore, the line segment OP is the shortest of all the distances of the point O to the points on the line XY.
We know from Euclidean geometry that the shortest distance between a point and a line is the perpendicular distance.

Therefore, OP ⊥ XY.
Hence Proved!
[ROUGH_WORK]
Shortest distance from point O to line XY is perpendicular. Since OP is radius and every other point on line is outside the circle, OP is strictly minimum!
Boxed Answer: [ OP ⊥ XY (Proved) ].
concept_questions: Why must any point Q on the tangent line other than the point of contact P lie strictly outside the circle?
What would happen to the perpendicularity property if a secant line rotated until its two intersection points coincided?
Can a radius be perpendicular to a chord at a point other than its midpoint or the point of contact?

common_misconceptions: Thinking a circle can have parallel tangents at adjacent points: A circle can only have parallel tangents at the diametrically opposite endpoints of a diameter!
Believing a tangent crosses inside the circle: By definition, a tangent touches the circle at exactly one point without entering the interior.

title: Tangents from an External Point: Theorem 10.2 Proof (PA = PB) & Angle Subtensions
description: Rigorously prove Theorem 10.2: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal. Master the two fundamental corollaries: (1) tangents subtend equal angles at the centre (∠AOP = ∠BOP), and (2) tangents are equally inclined to the line joining the point to the centre (∠APO = ∠BPO).
key_concepts: Theorem 10.2: The lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal (PA = PB)
RHS Congruence Proof: Hypotenuse OP is common; Radii OA = OB; Right angles ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90° (by Theorem 10.1)
Central Angle Bisector: OP bisects ∠AOB (∠AOP = ∠BOP)
External Angle Bisector: OP bisects ∠APB (∠APO = ∠BPO)

Supplementary Angle Theorem: The angle between the two tangents (∠APB) and the angle subtended by the line segment joining the points of contact at the centre (∠AOB) are supplementary: ∠APB + ∠AOB = 180°
subtopics: Formal statement and proof of Theorem 10.2
Proof of supplementary angles in cyclic/quadrilateral OAPB

worked_examples.given: A circle C(O, r) with centre O, a point P lying outside the circle, and two tangents PQ and PR drawn from point P touching the circle at Q and R respectively.
worked_examples.formula: RHS (Right-Hypotenuse-Side) Congruence Criterion and Theorem 10.1 (Radius ⊥ Tangent).
worked_examples.substitution: In right ΔOQP and right ΔORP: ∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90°, OP = OP (common hypotenuse), OQ = OR (radii). Therefore ΔOQP ≅ ΔORP.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. In ΔOQP and ΔORP:
   - ∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90° (By Theorem 10.1: radius ⊥ tangent at point of contact)
   - OP = OP (Common hypotenuse)
   - OQ = OR (Radii of the same circle)
2. By RHS Congruence Criterion, ΔOQP ≅ ΔORP.
3. By Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles (CPCT):
   PQ = PR.
4. Additionally, ∠OPQ = ∠OPR, showing that the line joining the external point to the centre bisects the angle between the two tangents.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: PQ = PR (Lengths of tangents from external point are equal)
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
A circle with centre O, an external point P, and two tangents PQ and PR touching the circle at Q and R respectively.

TO PROVE:
PQ = PR.

CONSTRUCTION:
Join OP, OQ, and OR.

PROOF:
Step 1: Establish right angles:
By Theorem 10.1, the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
Therefore:
OQ ⊥ PQ ⇒ ∠OQP = 90°
OR ⊥ PR ⇒ ∠ORP = 90°.

Step 2: Compare triangles ΔOQP and ΔORP:
In right-angled triangles ΔOQP and ΔORP:
- Hypotenuse OP = Hypotenuse OP  (Common side)
- Radius OQ = Radius OR          (Radii of the same circle)
- ∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90°             (Each right angle)

Step 3: Apply RHS Congruence:
By RHS (Right angle - Hypotenuse - Side) congruence criterion:
ΔOQP ≅ ΔORP.

Step 4: Conclude by CPCT:
Since corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal:
PQ = PR.

Hence Proved!

[ROUGH_WORK]
Alternative proof via Pythagoras Theorem:
PQ² = OP² - OQ² = OP² - OR² = PR² (since OQ = OR = r). Taking square root yields PQ = PR!
Boxed Answer: [ PQ = PR (Proved) ].

worked_examples.given: Two concentric circles C1 and C2 with common centre O. AB is a chord of the larger circle C1 which touches the smaller circle C2 at point P.
worked_examples.formula: Theorem 10.1 (Radius ⊥ Tangent) and the circle theorem: The perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
worked_examples.substitution: AB is tangent to C2 at P ⇒ OP ⊥ AB. In circle C1, AB is a chord and OP ⊥ AB ⇒ AP = BP.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Consider AB with respect to the smaller circle C2: AB is a tangent to C2 at point P, and OP is the radius of C2 through point of contact P. By Theorem 10.1, OP ⊥ AB.
2. Consider AB with respect to the larger circle C1: AB is a chord of circle C1, and OP is perpendicular from the centre O to chord AB (OP ⊥ AB).
3. By standard Euclidean circle theorem, the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.
4. Therefore, AP = BP.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: AP = BP (Chord AB is bisected at point of contact P)
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
Two concentric circles C1 and C2 with centre O.
AB is a chord of the larger circle C1 touching the smaller circle C2 at point P (Fig. 10.8).

TO PROVE:
AP = BP (i.e., chord AB is bisected at P).

CONSTRUCTION:
Join OP.

PROOF:
Step 1: Analyze line AB with respect to the smaller circle C2:
AB touches circle C2 at the single point P. Thus, AB is a tangent to C2 at point of contact P, and OP is the radius to that point.
By Theorem 10.1:
OP ⊥ AB.

Step 2: Analyze line segment AB with respect to the larger circle C1:
AB is a chord of the larger circle C1.
From Step 1, OP is perpendicular from the centre O to chord AB: OP ⊥ AB.
We know that the perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
Therefore:
AP = BP.

Hence Proved!

[ROUGH_WORK]
Key insight: A line is simultaneously a tangent to the inner circle (making OP ⊥ AB) and a chord to the outer circle (so OP ⊥ chord bisects it).
Boxed Answer: [ AP = BP (Proved) ].

How does the Pythagorean relation r² = R² - (chord/2)² connect the radii of the two concentric circles?

worked_examples.given: A circle with centre O, an external point T, and tangents TP and TQ touching the circle at P and Q respectively.
worked_examples.formula: Theorem 10.2 (TP = TQ), Angle Sum Property in ΔTPQ, and Theorem 10.1 (∠OPT = 90°).
worked_examples.substitution: Let ∠PTQ = θ. In isosceles ΔTPQ, ∠TPQ = (180° - θ)/2 = 90° - θ/2. Since ∠OPT = 90°, ∠OPQ = ∠OPT - ∠TPQ = 90° - (90° - θ/2) = θ/2.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. By Theorem 10.2, TP = TQ. Hence ΔTPQ is an isosceles triangle with ∠TPQ = ∠TQP.
2. In ΔTPQ: ∠PTQ + ∠TPQ + ∠TQP = 180° ⇒ θ + 2 ∠TPQ = 180° ⇒ ∠TPQ = 90° - θ/2.
3. By Theorem 10.1, radius OP ⊥ TP ⇒ ∠OPT = 90°.
4. Notice that ∠OPQ = ∠OPT - ∠TPQ = 90° - (90° - θ/2) = θ/2.
5. Therefore, 2 ∠OPQ = θ = ∠PTQ.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
A circle with centre O, an external point T, and tangents TP and TQ touching the circle at P and Q (Fig. 10.9).

TO PROVE:
∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.

PROOF:
Let ∠PTQ = θ.

Step 1: Analyze ΔTPQ:
By Theorem 10.2, the lengths of tangents drawn from an external point are equal:
TP = TQ.
Therefore, ΔTPQ is an isosceles triangle with TP = TQ.
In an isosceles triangle, angles opposite to equal sides are equal:
∠TPQ = ∠TQP.

Step 2: Use Angle Sum Property in ΔTPQ:
∠PTQ + ∠TPQ + ∠TQP = 180°
θ + 2 ∠TPQ = 180°
2 ∠TPQ = 180° - θ
∠TPQ = (180° - θ) / 2 = 90° - θ/2   ... (1)

Step 3: Relate to radius OP:
By Theorem 10.1, the radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent TP at point P:
∠OPT = 90°.
Notice that ∠OPT = ∠OPQ + ∠TPQ:
∠OPQ + ∠TPQ = 90°
∠OPQ = 90° - ∠TPQ.

Step 4: Substitute ∠TPQ from equation (1):
∠OPQ = 90° - (90° - θ/2)
∠OPQ = 90° - 90° + θ/2
∠OPQ = θ / 2.
Multiply both sides by 2:
2 ∠OPQ = θ.
Since θ = ∠PTQ:
∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ.

Hence Proved!

[ROUGH_WORK]
Key insight: In isosceles ΔTPQ, base angle is 90° - θ/2. Since radius OP ⊥ TP (90°), the remaining angle ∠OPQ is exactly θ/2!
Boxed Answer: [ ∠PTQ = 2 ∠OPQ (Proved) ].

worked_examples.given: Circle with centre O and radius OP = 5 cm. Chord PQ = 8 cm. Tangents TP and TQ intersect at T. Line OT intersects chord PQ at R.
worked_examples.formula: OT is the perpendicular bisector of chord PQ. In right ΔOPR, PR = 4 cm, OR = √(OP² - PR²). By similarity of right triangles ΔTPR ~ ΔOPR, TP/PO = PR/RO.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. OT bisects chord PQ perpendicularly at R. Therefore PR = RQ = 8/2 = 4 cm, and ∠PRO = 90°.
2. In right ΔOPR: OR = √(OP² - PR²) = √(5² - 4²) = 3 cm.
3. In right ΔOPT (∠OPT = 90°), PR ⊥ OT. Triangles ΔTPR and ΔOPR are both right-angled and complementary: ∠TPR = 90° - ∠RPT = ∠POR.
4. Therefore, ΔTPR ~ ΔOPR (AA similarity).
5. Taking ratio of corresponding sides: TP / PO = PR / RO ⇒ TP / 5 = 4 / 3 ⇒ TP = (5 × 4) / 3 = 20/3 cm = 6.67 cm.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
A circle with centre O and radius OP = OQ = 5 cm.
A chord PQ of length 8 cm.
Tangents at P and Q meet at external point T (Fig. 10.10).

TO FIND:
Length of tangent TP.

STEP-BY-STEP CALCULATION:
Step 1: Geometric symmetry of line OT:
By Theorem 10.2, TP = TQ. Also OP = OQ = 5 cm.
Therefore, OT is the perpendicular bisector of the chord PQ.
Let OT intersect chord PQ at point R.
Then:
PR = RQ = PQ / 2 = 8 / 2 = 4 cm,
and ∠PRO = ∠PRT = 90°.

Step 2: Find OR using Pythagoras Theorem in right ΔPRO:
In right ΔPRO:
OP² = PR² + OR²
5² = 4² + OR²
25 = 16 + OR²
OR² = 25 - 16 = 9
OR = 3 cm.

Step 3: Relate right triangles using similarity:
In right ΔOPT (∠OPT = 90° by Theorem 10.1):
∠TPR + ∠RPO = 90°.
Also in right ΔPRO:
∠POR + ∠RPO = 90°.
Equating both:
∠TPR = ∠POR.
Now compare right triangles ΔTPR and ΔOPR:
- ∠PRT = ∠PRO = 90°
- ∠TPR = ∠POR (Proved above)
By AA similarity criterion:
ΔTPR ~ ΔOPR.

Step 4: Form side proportion:
TP / PO = PR / RO
Substitute the known values:
TP / 5 = 4 / 3
TP = (4 × 5) / 3 = 20 / 3 cm.

[ROUGH_WORK]
Alternative via algebra: Let TP = x, TR = y. In right ΔPRT: x² = y² + 4² = y² + 16. In right ΔOPT: x² + 5² = (y + 3)². (y² + 16) + 25 = y² + 6y + 9 ⇒ 41 = 6y + 9 ⇒ 6y = 32 ⇒ y = 16/3. Then x² = (16/3)² + 16 = 256/9 + 144/9 = 400/9 ⇒ x = 20/3 cm!
Boxed Answer: [ 20/3 cm ].

title: Exercise 10.1 & Exercise 10.2 Part 1 Solver: Contact Computations & Parallel Tangents (Q1 to Q5)
description: Complete step-by-step resolution of NCERT Exercise 10.1 (all 4 questions) and Exercise 10.2 Questions 1 through 5. Covers tangent distance computations using Pythagoras theorem (OQ = 12 cm, r = 5 cm ⇒ PQ = √119 cm), angle calculations (∠POQ = 110° ⇒ ∠PTQ = 70°), proof that tangents at ends of diameter are parallel, and proof that perpendicular at contact point passes through centre.
key_concepts: Ex 10.1 Q1-Q4: Circle has infinitely many tangents; secant cuts in 2 points; circle can have at most 2 parallel tangents in a given direction
Ex 10.1 Q3: Right ΔOPQ with OP = 5 cm, OQ = 12 cm ⇒ PQ = √(12² - 5²) = √(144 - 25) = √119 cm
Ex 10.2 Q1: Point Q at 25 cm from center, tangent length 24 cm ⇒ Radius r = √(25² - 24²) = √(625 - 576) = √49 = 7 cm
Ex 10.2 Q2: TP and TQ tangents with ∠POQ = 110° ⇒ ∠PTQ = 180° - 110° = 70° (Supplementary angles)
Ex 10.2 Q3: Tangents PA and PB inclined at 80° ⇒ ∠AOB = 100° ⇒ ∠POA = 100° / 2 = 50°
Ex 10.2 Q4: Tangents at diameter ends AB: Radii OA ⊥ Tangent 1 and OB ⊥ Tangent 2 ⇒ Alternate interior angles are equal (90° = 90°) ⇒ Tangents are strictly parallel!
Ex 10.2 Q5: Perpendicular at point of contact passes through centre (Proof by contradiction)

Full resolution of Exercise 10.2 Q1 to Q5

worked_examples.problem: [NCERT Class 10 Ch 10 | Section 10.2 | Page 147] Exercise 10.1 Q1: How many tangents can a circle have?
worked_examples.section: 10.2 Tangent to a Circle
worked_examples.given: A circle in a Euclidean two-dimensional plane.
worked_examples.formula: A circle consists of infinitely many points on its circumference, and at each point exactly one unique tangent can be drawn.
worked_examples.substitution: Number of points on circle = ∞ ⇒ Number of tangents = ∞.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. A circle is the locus of points equidistant from a central point, containing infinitely many points.
2. By Theorem 10.1, at every single point on the circle, a distinct perpendicular line to the radius at that point can be constructed.
3. Each such line touches the circle at exactly one point, thus forming a unique tangent.
4. Therefore, a circle can have infinitely many tangents.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
A circle in a Euclidean plane.

TO FIND:
The number of tangents a circle can have.

FORMULA USED:
A circle consists of infinitely many points along its perimeter, and at each point on the circumference, exactly one tangent can be drawn perpendicular to the radius.

STEP-BY-STEP CALCULATION:
1. A circle is composed of infinitely many points on its circumference.
2. At each individual point on the circle, exactly one unique line can be drawn that is perpendicular to the radius through that point.
3. Each such perpendicular line meets the circle at exactly one point, satisfying the definition of a tangent line.
4. Because there are infinitely many points on the circle, there are infinitely many such tangents.

[ROUGH_WORK]
Points on circle = ∞. Each point yields 1 unique tangent. Total tangents = ∞.
Boxed Answer: [ Infinitely many ].

worked_examples.section: 10.2 Tangent to a Circle
worked_examples.given: Four geometric statements regarding circles, tangents, and secants.
worked_examples.formula: Definitions from Section 10.1 and 10.2 of NCERT Class 10.
worked_examples.substitution: (i) one; (ii) secant; (iii) two; (iv) point of contact.
worked_examples.calculation:
Part (i): A tangent line touches the circle at exactly one point.
Part (ii): A line intersecting the circle in two distinct points is defined as a secant.
Part (iii): For any given direction/tangent line, only the tangent at the diametrically opposite point can be parallel to it, giving at most 2 parallel tangents.
Part (iv): The common intersection point between the circle and the tangent is termed the point of contact.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (i) one, (ii) secant, (iii) two, (iv) point of contact
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
Four fundamental geometric statements on circles and straight lines.

TO FIND:
The exact mathematical terms for each blank.

STEP-BY-STEP CALCULATION / PROOF:
(i) By definition, a tangent to a circle intersects the circle in exactly ONE point.
(ii) A line that intersects a circle in two distinct points is called a SECANT.
(iii) Parallel tangents can only be drawn at the two opposite endpoints of a diameter. Therefore, a circle can have TWO parallel tangents at the most for any given line orientation.
(iv) The common point of the tangent and the circle is called the POINT OF CONTACT.

[ROUGH_WORK]
Key vocabulary: Tangent -> 1 point; Secant -> 2 points; Max parallel tangents = 2 (at diameter ends); Intersection = Point of Contact.
Boxed Answer: [ (i) one, (ii) secant, (iii) two, (iv) point of contact ].

worked_examples.given: Circle with centre O and radius OP = 5 cm. Tangent PQ touches at P. Distance OQ = 12 cm.
worked_examples.formula: In right ΔOPQ, by Theorem 10.1, ∠OPQ = 90°. By Pythagoras Theorem: OQ² = OP² + PQ².
worked_examples.calculation: PQ = √119 cm.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
A circle with centre O and radius OP = 5 cm.
A tangent PQ touches the circle at point P.
Line through centre O meets tangent at Q such that OQ = 12 cm.

TO FIND:
Length of segment PQ.

FORMULA USED:
By Theorem 10.1, the radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent PQ at the point of contact P:
∠OPQ = 90°.
In right triangle OPQ, by Pythagoras Theorem:
OQ² = OP² + PQ².

STEP-BY-STEP CALCULATION:
Step 1: Apply Pythagoras theorem in right ΔOPQ:
OQ² = OP² + PQ²
Step 2: Substitute the known values:
12² = 5² + PQ²
144 = 25 + PQ²
Step 3: Solve for PQ²:
PQ² = 144 - 25 = 119
Step 4: Take the positive square root:
PQ = √119 cm.

Thus, option (D) is correct.

[ROUGH_WORK]
Right triangle with hypotenuse OQ = 12, leg OP = 5. PQ = √(12² - 5²) = √(144 - 25) = √119.
Boxed Answer: [ √119 cm (Option D) ].

worked_examples.problem: [NCERT Class 10 Ch 10 | Section 10.2 | Page 147] Exercise 10.1 Q4: Draw a circle and two lines parallel to a given line such that one is a tangent and the other, a secant to the circle.
worked_examples.section: 10.2 Tangent to a Circle
worked_examples.given: A circle with centre O and a given straight line l in the same plane.
worked_examples.formula: A line parallel to line l passing through a point on the circle at distance r from O is a tangent; a line parallel to line l passing at distance d < r from O is a secant.
worked_examples.substitution: Draw diameter AB perpendicular to given line l. Construct tangent through A parallel to l, and secant through internal point C on AB parallel to l.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Draw a circle with centre O and a given line l outside the circle.
2. Draw a line m perpendicular to line l passing through centre O, intersecting the circle at points A and B.
3. Through point A (on the circle), draw line p perpendicular to line m. Since p ⊥ m and l ⊥ m, p ∥ l. Since p touches the circle at exactly one point A, line p is a TANGENT parallel to line l.
4. Choose a point C on segment OA between O and A. Through point C, draw line q perpendicular to line m. Line q ∥ l. Since C is inside the circle, line q intersects the circle in two distinct points, making line q a SECANT parallel to line l.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Construction completed with line p as tangent parallel to line l, and line q as secant parallel to line l.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
A circle with centre O and a given straight reference line l.

TO CONSTRUCT:
Two lines parallel to line l such that one is a tangent and the other is a secant to the circle.

STEP-BY-STEP CONSTRUCTION / PROOF:
1. Draw a circle with centre O and draw a reference straight line l.
2. From centre O, draw a perpendicular to line l, meeting line l at point N. Let this perpendicular ray intersect the circle at point A and diameter at B.
3. At point A (which lies on the circle), construct a line p perpendicular to ON. Since p ⊥ ON and l ⊥ ON, line p is parallel to line l (p ∥ l). By Theorem 10.1, since OA is a radius and p ⊥ OA at A, line p touches the circle at exactly one point A. Hence, line p is a TANGENT parallel to line l.
4. Take any point C on the radius OA inside the circle (between O and A). Construct a line q perpendicular to ON at C. Since q ⊥ ON and l ⊥ ON, line q is parallel to line l (q ∥ l). Since point C lies strictly inside the circle, line q intersects the circle at two distinct points. Hence, line q is a SECANT parallel to line l.

[ROUGH_WORK]
Perpendicular from O to given line gives diameter axis. Tangent at point on circumference is parallel. Secant at any internal point is parallel.
Boxed Answer: [ Line p (Tangent) ∥ Line q (Secant) ∥ Line l (Constructed) ].

worked_examples.given: Length of tangent from point Q is PQ = 24 cm. Distance of Q from centre O is OQ = 25 cm.
worked_examples.formula: By Theorem 10.1, radius OP ⊥ PQ. By Pythagoras Theorem: OQ² = OP² + PQ².
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
Let O be the centre of the circle and P be the point of contact of the tangent from external point Q.
Length of tangent PQ = 24 cm.
Distance of point Q from the centre OQ = 25 cm.

TO FIND:
Radius of the circle (OP).

FORMULA USED:
By Theorem 10.1, the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact:
∠OPQ = 90°.
In right triangle OPQ, by Pythagoras Theorem:
OQ² = OP² + PQ².

STEP-BY-STEP CALCULATION:
1. Apply Pythagoras Theorem in right ΔOPQ:
   OQ² = OP² + PQ²
2. Substitute the values:
   25² = OP² + 24²
   625 = OP² + 576
3. Solve for OP²:
   OP² = 625 - 576 = 49
4. Take the positive square root:
   OP = √49 = 7 cm.

Therefore, the correct option is (A).

[ROUGH_WORK]
Pythagorean triplet (7, 24, 25). 25² - 24² = (25-24)(25+24) = 1 × 49 = 49. √49 = 7.
Boxed Answer: [ 7 cm (Option A) ].

worked_examples.formula: Sum of angles of quadrilateral OPTQ is 360°. By Theorem 10.1, ∠OPT = ∠OQT = 90°.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
TP and TQ are tangents to a circle with centre O from external point T.
∠POQ = 110° (Fig. 10.11).

TO FIND:
Measure of ∠PTQ.

FORMULA USED:
By Theorem 10.1, the radius through the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent:
OP ⊥ TP ⇒ ∠OPT = 90°
OQ ⊥ TQ ⇒ ∠OQT = 90°.
The sum of all interior angles of a quadrilateral is 360°.

STEP-BY-STEP CALCULATION:
1. Consider quadrilateral OPTQ:
   ∠OPT + ∠POQ + ∠OQT + ∠PTQ = 360°
2. Substitute the known angle measures:
   90° + 110° + 90° + ∠PTQ = 360°
3. Simplify the sum:
   290° + ∠PTQ = 360°
4. Solve for ∠PTQ:
   ∠PTQ = 360° - 290° = 70°.

Therefore, option (B) is the correct answer.

[ROUGH_WORK]
Opposite angles in cyclic quadrilateral formed by tangents: ∠PTQ + ∠POQ = 180° (supplementary). ∠PTQ = 180° - 110° = 70°.
Boxed Answer: [ 70° (Option B) ].

worked_examples.given: Tangents PA and PB from external point P to circle with centre O are inclined at ∠APB = 80°.
worked_examples.formula: ∠AOB + ∠APB = 180° (supplementary). Line OP bisects ∠AOB: ∠POA = ∠AOB / 2.
worked_examples.substitution: ∠AOB = 180° - 80° = 100°. In congruent ΔOAP and ΔOBP, ∠POA = 100° / 2 = 50°.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. In quadrilateral OAPB: ∠OAP = 90°, ∠OBP = 90°, ∠APB = 80°.
2. ∠AOB = 360° - (90° + 90° + 80°) = 100°.
3. ΔOAP ≅ ΔOBP by RHS criterion, so ∠POA = ∠POB = 100° / 2 = 50°.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
PA and PB are tangents from point P to a circle with centre O.
Angle between the tangents ∠APB = 80°.

TO FIND:
Measure of ∠POA.

STEP-BY-STEP CALCULATION:
Step 1: Use quadrilateral OAPB:
By Theorem 10.1:
OA ⊥ PA ⇒ ∠OAP = 90°
OB ⊥ PB ⇒ ∠OBP = 90°.
In quadrilateral OAPB:
∠AOB + ∠OAP + ∠APB + ∠OBP = 360°
∠AOB + 90° + 80° + 90° = 360°
∠AOB + 260° = 360°
∠AOB = 360° - 260° = 100°.

Step 2: Use congruence of ΔOAP and ΔOBP:
In ΔOAP and ΔOBP:
- OA = OB (radii)
- OP = OP (common hypotenuse)
- ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90°
By RHS congruence:
ΔOAP ≅ ΔOBP.
Therefore, by CPCT:
∠POA = ∠POB.

Step 3: Calculate ∠POA:
Since ∠POA + ∠POB = ∠AOB = 100°:
2 ∠POA = 100°
∠POA = 100° / 2 = 50°.

Therefore, option (A) is correct.

[ROUGH_WORK]
Direct shortcut: In right ΔOAP, ∠APO = 80°/2 = 40°. Since ∠OAP = 90°, ∠POA = 90° - 40° = 50°!
Boxed Answer: [ 50° (Option A) ].

worked_examples.problem: [NCERT Class 10 Ch 10 | Section 10.3 | Page 152] Exercise 10.2 Q4: Prove that the tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are parallel.
worked_examples.section: 10.3 Number of Tangents from a Point on a Circle
worked_examples.given: A circle with centre O and diameter AB. Lines PQ and RS are tangents to the circle at the endpoints A and B of the diameter respectively.
worked_examples.formula: Theorem 10.1 (Radius ⊥ Tangent) and the Alternate Interior Angles Converse theorem for parallel lines.
worked_examples.substitution: OA ⊥ PQ ⇒ ∠PAB = 90°. OB ⊥ RS ⇒ ∠ABS = 90°. Alternate interior angles ∠PAB = ∠ABS = 90° ⇒ PQ ∥ RS.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. AB is a diameter passing through centre O, so OA and OB are radii lying along the same straight line AB.
2. Tangent PQ touches the circle at A. By Theorem 10.1, radius OA ⊥ PQ, so ∠PAB = 90° (and ∠QAB = 90°).
3. Tangent RS touches the circle at B. By Theorem 10.1, radius OB ⊥ RS, so ∠ABS = 90° (and ∠ABR = 90°).
4. Considering line AB as a transversal intersecting lines PQ and RS:
   ∠PAB and ∠ABS are alternate interior angles, and ∠PAB = ∠ABS = 90°.
5. Since the alternate interior angles are equal, line PQ must be parallel to line RS (PQ ∥ RS).
worked_examples.finalAnswer: PQ ∥ RS (Tangents at ends of diameter are parallel)
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
A circle with centre O and diameter AB.
PQ is the tangent drawn at point A.
RS is the tangent drawn at point B.

TO PROVE:
PQ ∥ RS.

PROOF:
Step 1: Apply Theorem 10.1 at point A:
Since OA is a radius and PQ is the tangent at A:
OA ⊥ PQ
⇒ ∠PAB = 90°   ... (1)

Step 2: Apply Theorem 10.1 at point B:
Since OB is a radius and RS is the tangent at B:
OB ⊥ RS
⇒ ∠ABS = 90°   ... (2)

Step 3: Analyze transversal AB:
Line segment AB acts as a transversal line intersecting lines PQ and RS.
From (1) and (2):
∠PAB = ∠ABS = 90°.
Notice that ∠PAB and ∠ABS form a pair of alternate interior angles.
By Euclidean geometry, if a pair of alternate interior angles formed by a transversal intersecting two lines are equal, then the two lines are parallel.

Therefore:
PQ ∥ RS.

Hence Proved!

[ROUGH_WORK]
Both angles are 90° because radius ⊥ tangent. Consecutive interior angles also sum to 90° + 90° = 180°, which also proves PQ ∥ RS.
Boxed Answer: [ PQ ∥ RS (Proved) ].

worked_examples.problem: [NCERT Class 10 Ch 10 | Section 10.3 | Page 152] Exercise 10.2 Q5: Prove that the perpendicular at the point of contact to the tangent to a circle passes through the centre.
worked_examples.section: 10.3 Number of Tangents from a Point on a Circle
worked_examples.image_search_query: tangent perpendicular point of contact centre proof
worked_examples.given: A circle with centre O and a tangent line AB touching the circle at point P.
worked_examples.formula: Proof by contradiction (Reductio ad absurdum) using Theorem 10.1.
worked_examples.substitution: Assume perpendicular at P is line PQ passing through O' ≠ O. Then ∠O'PB = 90°. By Theorem 10.1, ∠OPB = 90°. Hence ∠O'PB = ∠OPB, which is impossible unless line PO' coincides with line PO.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Let AB be tangent to circle C(O, r) at point P.
2. By Theorem 10.1, the radius OP is perpendicular to the tangent line AB at P. Hence ∠OPB = 90°.
3. Suppose, if possible, that the perpendicular to AB at P does not pass through centre O. Let it pass through some other point O' ≠ O. Then line O'P ⊥ AB, which implies ∠O'PB = 90°.
4. Comparing both gives ∠O'PB = ∠OPB.
5. From the geometry of rays, a part cannot equal the whole unless ray PO' and ray PO coincide.
6. Hence, the perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact must pass through the centre O.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: The perpendicular to the tangent at the point of contact passes through the centre.
worked_examples.solution:
STATEMENT:
Prove that the perpendicular at the point of contact to the tangent to a circle passes through the centre.

GIVEN:
A circle with centre O and a tangent line AB touching the circle at point P.

TO PROVE:
The perpendicular to AB at point P passes through centre O.

PROOF (By Contradiction):
Step 1: Direct fact from Theorem 10.1:
By Theorem 10.1, the radius through the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent:
OP ⊥ AB
Therefore, ∠OPB = 90°   ... (1)

Step 2: Assume contradiction:
Let us assume, on the contrary, that the perpendicular to AB at point P does not pass through centre O.
Suppose it passes through another distinct point O'.
Then line O'P is perpendicular to AB:
O'P ⊥ AB
Therefore, ∠O'PB = 90°   ... (2)

Step 3: Analyze the contradiction:
From equations (1) and (2):
∠O'PB = ∠OPB.
However, looking at the figure, point O' is distinct from O, which means line O'P lies inside (or outside) ∠OPB, making ∠O'PB a proper part of ∠OPB.
A part cannot equal the whole (Euclid's common notion).
This equality ∠O'PB = ∠OPB is possible ONLY IF the ray PO' coincides exactly with ray PO.

Step 4: Conclusion:
Therefore, our assumption was false. The perpendicular to the tangent AB at the point of contact P must pass through the centre O.
Hence Proved!

[ROUGH_WORK]
Uniqueness of perpendicular at a point on a straight line: at point P on line AB, there can only be ONE perpendicular ray. Since OP is already perpendicular (90°), any perpendicular must lie along OP!
Boxed Answer: [ Perpendicular at P passes through centre O (Proved) ].

worked_examples.given: Distance of point A from centre O is OA = 5 cm. Length of tangent from A touching circle at P is AP = 4 cm.
worked_examples.formula: By Theorem 10.1, radius OP ⊥ tangent AP (∠OPA = 90°). In right ΔOPA, OA² = OP² + AP².
worked_examples.calculation: OP = √9 = 3 cm.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
Let O be the centre of the circle.
Point A is at a distance of OA = 5 cm from the centre.
Let P be the point of contact of the tangent drawn from A to the circle.
Length of tangent AP = 4 cm.

TO FIND:
Radius of the circle (OP).

FORMULA USED:
By Theorem 10.1, the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact:
OP ⊥ AP ⇒ ∠OPA = 90°.
In right triangle OPA, by Pythagoras Theorem:
OA² = OP² + AP².

STEP-BY-STEP CALCULATION:
1. Apply Pythagoras Theorem in right ΔOPA:
   OA² = OP² + AP²
2. Substitute the given values:
   5² = OP² + 4²
   25 = OP² + 16
3. Solve for OP²:
   OP² = 25 - 16 = 9
4. Take the positive square root:
   OP = √9 = 3 cm.

[ROUGH_WORK]
Right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 5 and leg 4. Other leg is √(5² - 4²) = 3 cm.
Boxed Answer: [ 3 cm ].

worked_examples.given: Two concentric circles with common centre O. Outer radius R = 5 cm, inner radius r = 3 cm. Chord AB of outer circle touches inner circle at P.
worked_examples.formula: By Theorem 10.1, OP ⊥ AB. In right ΔOPA, OA² = OP² + AP². Also, perpendicular from centre bisects chord: AB = 2 × AP.
worked_examples.substitution: 5² = 3² + AP² ⇒ 25 = 9 + AP² ⇒ AP² = 16 ⇒ AP = 4 cm. AB = 2 × 4 = 8 cm.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. In right ΔOPA: AP = √(5² - 3²) = √(25 - 9) = √16 = 4 cm.
2. Since OP ⊥ chord AB in the outer circle, OP bisects AB, so AB = 2 × AP = 2 × 4 = 8 cm.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
Two concentric circles C1 and C2 with common centre O.
Radius of larger circle OA = 5 cm.
Radius of smaller circle OP = 3 cm.
AB is a chord of the larger circle C1 that touches the smaller circle C2 at point P.

TO FIND:
Length of the chord AB.

FORMULA USED:
1. By Theorem 10.1, the radius of C2 is perpendicular to tangent AB: OP ⊥ AB (∠OPA = 90°).
2. By Pythagoras Theorem in right ΔOPA: OA² = OP² + AP².
3. The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord: AB = 2 × AP.

STEP-BY-STEP CALCULATION:
Step 1: Calculate AP using right ΔOPA:
In right ΔOPA:
OA² = OP² + AP²
5² = 3² + AP²
25 = 9 + AP²
AP² = 25 - 9 = 16
AP = √16 = 4 cm.

Step 2: Find total length of chord AB:
Since OP ⊥ AB and AB is a chord of the larger circle C1, the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord:
AP = PB
AB = 2 × AP = 2 × 4 = 8 cm.

[ROUGH_WORK]
Hypotenuse = 5, vertical leg = 3 ⇒ base leg = 4 cm. Total chord = 4 + 4 = 8 cm.
Boxed Answer: [ 8 cm ].

worked_examples.substitution: From vertex A: AP = AS (1). From vertex B: BP = BQ (2). From vertex C: CR = CQ (3). From vertex D: DR = DS (4).
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Add equations (1) + (2) + (3) + (4):
   (AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ)
2. Since AP + BP = AB, CR + DR = CD, AS + DS = AD, BQ + CQ = BC:
   AB + CD = AD + BC.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
A quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle with centre O.
The sides AB, BC, CD, and DA touch the circle at points P, Q, R, and S respectively (Fig. 10.12).

TO PROVE:
AB + CD = AD + BC.

PROOF:
By Theorem 10.2, the lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.

Step 1: Write tangent equalities from each of the four vertices:
- From external point A: AP and AS are tangents to the circle:
  AP = AS   ... (1)
- From external point B: BP and BQ are tangents to the circle:
  BP = BQ   ... (2)
- From external point C: CR and CQ are tangents to the circle:
  CR = CQ   ... (3)
- From external point D: DR and DS are tangents to the circle:
  DR = DS   ... (4)

Step 2: Add equations (1), (2), (3), and (4) together:
LHS = AP + BP + CR + DR
RHS = AS + BQ + CQ + DS

Step 3: Group terms representing opposite sides:
LHS = (AP + BP) + (CR + DR)
Since AP + BP = AB and CR + DR = CD:
LHS = AB + CD.

RHS = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ)
Since AS + DS = AD and BQ + CQ = BC:
RHS = AD + BC.

Equating LHS and RHS:
AB + CD = AD + BC.

Hence Proved!

[ROUGH_WORK]
Crucial alignment: Keep segments belonging to AB and CD on the left, and segments belonging to AD and BC on the right so they sum cleanly to full sides!
Boxed Answer: [ AB + CD = AD + BC (Proved) ].

worked_examples.given: XY ∥ X'Y' are parallel tangents to a circle with centre O touching at P and Q (so POQ is a diameter). Tangent AB touches the circle at C, intersecting XY at A and X'Y' at B (Fig. 10.13).
worked_examples.formula: SSS Congruence of triangles and Linear Pair Axiom along straight diameter POQ.
worked_examples.substitution: ΔOPA ≅ ΔOCA ⇒ ∠POA = ∠COA. ΔOQB ≅ ΔOCB ⇒ ∠QOB = ∠COB. Since ∠POQ = 180°: 2∠COA + 2∠COB = 180° ⇒ ∠COA + ∠COB = 90°.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. In ΔOPA and ΔOCA: OP = OC (radii), AP = AC (tangents from A), OA = OA (common). By SSS, ΔOPA ≅ ΔOCA. Hence ∠POA = ∠COA.
2. In ΔOQB and ΔOCB: OQ = OC (radii), BQ = BC (tangents from B), OB = OB (common). By SSS, ΔOQB ≅ ΔOCB. Hence ∠QOB = ∠COB.
3. Since POQ is a diameter (straight line): ∠POA + ∠COA + ∠COB + ∠QOB = 180°.
4. 2 ∠COA + 2 ∠COB = 180° ⇒ 2 (∠COA + ∠COB) = 180° ⇒ ∠AOB = 90°.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
XY and X'Y' are two parallel tangents to a circle with centre O, touching at P and Q respectively.
Line segment POQ is a diameter of the circle.
A third tangent AB with point of contact C intersects XY at A and X'Y' at B (Fig. 10.13).

TO PROVE:
∠AOB = 90°.

CONSTRUCTION:
Join OC.

PROOF:
Step 1: Prove ΔOPA ≅ ΔOCA:
In ΔOPA and ΔOCA:
- OP = OC  (Radii of the same circle)
- AP = AC  (Tangents from external point A to the circle, Theorem 10.2)
- OA = OA  (Common side)
By SSS congruence criterion:
ΔOPA ≅ ΔOCA.
Therefore, by CPCT:
∠POA = ∠COA   ... (1)

Step 2: Prove ΔOQB ≅ ΔOCB:
In ΔOQB and ΔOCB:
- OQ = OC  (Radii of the same circle)
- BQ = BC  (Tangents from external point B to the circle, Theorem 10.2)
- OB = OB  (Common side)
By SSS congruence criterion:
ΔOQB ≅ ΔOCB.
Therefore, by CPCT:
∠QOB = ∠COB   ... (2)

Step 3: Apply the straight line angle property on diameter POQ:
Since POQ is a straight diameter line passing through centre O:
∠POQ = 180°
∠POA + ∠COA + ∠COB + ∠QOB = 180°.

Step 4: Substitute from (1) and (2):
Since ∠POA = ∠COA and ∠QOB = ∠COB:
∠COA + ∠COA + ∠COB + ∠COB = 180°
2 ∠COA + 2 ∠COB = 180°
2 (∠COA + ∠COB) = 180°
∠COA + ∠COB = 180° / 2 = 90°.

Notice from the figure that ∠COA + ∠COB = ∠AOB.
Therefore:
∠AOB = 90°.

Hence Proved!

[ROUGH_WORK]
Alternative via interior angles: ∠PAC + ∠QBC = 180° (co-interior angles for XY ∥ X'Y'). AO and BO are angle bisectors, so ∠OAC + ∠OBC = 180°/2 = 90°. In ΔAOB, sum of angles is 180°, so ∠AOB = 180° - 90° = 90°!
Boxed Answer: [ ∠AOB = 90° (Proved) ].

title: Exercise 10.2 Part 3 Solver: Supplementary Angles, Rhombus Proofs & Circumscribed Triangles (Q10 to Q13)
description: Complete, rigorous step-by-step resolution of NCERT Exercise 10.2 Questions 10 through 13. Prove angle between tangents is supplementary to central angle (Q10), prove parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus (Q11), solve the master circumscribed triangle problem with radius 4 cm and segments 6 cm and 8 cm to find sides AB = 15 cm and AC = 13 cm via Heron's formula (Q12), and prove opposite sides of circumscribed quad subtend supplementary angles at centre (Q13).
key_concepts: Ex 10.2 Q10: Quadrilateral OAPB has ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90° ⇒ ∠APB + ∠AOB = 360° - 180° = 180° (Supplementary!)
Ex 10.2 Q11: Parallelogram ABCD circumscribing circle: AB = CD and AD = BC; from Q8, AB + CD = AD + BC ⇒ 2AB = 2AD ⇒ AB = AD ⇒ All 4 sides equal ⇒ ABCD is a Rhombus!

Ex 10.2 Q12: ΔABC circumscribes circle radius r = 4 cm; CD = 6 cm, BD = 8 cm ⇒ Let AF = AE = x ⇒ Sides are 14, 8+x, 6+x ⇒ Area by Heron's formula = Area of 3 sub-triangles ⇒ x = 7 ⇒ AB = 15 cm, AC = 13 cm
Ex 10.2 Q13: Opposite sides of circumscribed quadrilateral subtend supplementary angles at centre: ∠AOB + ∠COD = 180° and ∠AOD + ∠BOC = 180°
subtopics: Full resolution of Q10 to Q13 with complete geometric proofs
Full Heron's formula algebraic derivation for triangle sides in Q12
Proof of supplementary opposite central angles (Q13)

worked_examples.given: Tangents PA and PB drawn from external point P touch circle with centre O at points of contact A and B.
worked_examples.formula: Theorem 10.1 (OA ⊥ PA, OB ⊥ PB) and sum of interior angles of quadrilateral OAPB = 360°.
worked_examples.substitution: ∠OAP = 90°, ∠OBP = 90°. In quadrilateral OAPB: ∠APB + ∠AOB + 90° + 90° = 360° ⇒ ∠APB + ∠AOB = 180°.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. By Theorem 10.1, radius OA ⊥ tangent PA at A, so ∠OAP = 90°.
2. Similarly, radius OB ⊥ tangent PB at B, so ∠OBP = 90°.
3. In quadrilateral OAPB, the sum of all 4 interior angles is 360°:
   ∠APB + ∠AOB + ∠OAP + ∠OBP = 360°
4. Substitute ∠OAP = 90° and ∠OBP = 90°:
   ∠APB + ∠AOB + 180° = 360° ⇒ ∠APB + ∠AOB = 180°.
5. Since their sum is 180°, ∠APB and ∠AOB are supplementary.
worked_examples.solution:
STATEMENT:
Prove that the angle between the two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle is supplementary to the angle subtended by the line-segment joining the points of contact at the centre.

GIVEN:
A circle with centre O.
PA and PB are two tangents drawn from external point P to the circle, touching at points A and B respectively.
Line-segment AB joins the points of contact, subtending ∠AOB at centre O.

TO PROVE:
∠APB + ∠AOB = 180° (i.e., ∠APB and ∠AOB are supplementary).

PROOF:
Step 1: Use Theorem 10.1:
By Theorem 10.1, the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
Therefore:
OA ⊥ PA ⇒ ∠OAP = 90°   ... (1)
OB ⊥ PB ⇒ ∠OBP = 90°   ... (2)

Step 2: Apply the Angle Sum Property of Quadrilateral OAPB:
In quadrilateral OAPB:
∠APB + ∠AOB + ∠OAP + ∠OBP = 360°

Step 3: Substitute equations (1) and (2):
∠APB + ∠AOB + 90° + 90° = 360°
∠APB + ∠AOB + 180° = 360°
∠APB + ∠AOB = 360° - 180°
∠APB + ∠AOB = 180°.

Conclusion:
Since the sum of ∠APB and ∠AOB is 180°, the two angles are supplementary.
Hence Proved!

[ROUGH_WORK]
Two opposite angles of quadrilateral OAPB are each 90°, so their sum is 180°. Consequently, the remaining two opposite angles must also sum to 360° - 180° = 180°!
Boxed Answer: [ ∠APB + ∠AOB = 180° (Supplementary) (Proved) ].

worked_examples.given: A parallelogram ABCD circumscribes a circle, with sides touching at P, Q, R, and S.
worked_examples.formula: From Q8: AB + CD = AD + BC. In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal: AB = CD and AD = BC.
worked_examples.substitution: AB + AB = AD + AD ⇒ 2 AB = 2 AD ⇒ AB = AD. Since adjacent sides of parallelogram are equal, all sides are equal: AB = BC = CD = DA.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Let ABCD be a parallelogram circumscribing a circle. Opposite sides are equal: AB = CD and AD = BC.
2. By Theorem 10.2 (as proved in Exercise 10.2 Q8), for any circumscribing quadrilateral:
   AB + CD = AD + BC.
3. Substitute CD = AB and BC = AD:
   AB + AB = AD + AD
   2 AB = 2 AD ⇒ AB = AD.
4. Since adjacent sides AB and AD are equal in parallelogram ABCD:
   AB = BC = CD = DA.
5. A parallelogram with all four sides equal is a rhombus.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: Parallelogram ABCD is a rhombus (AB = BC = CD = DA)
worked_examples.solution:
STATEMENT:
Prove that the parallelogram circumscribing a circle is a rhombus.

GIVEN:
A parallelogram ABCD circumscribes a circle with centre O.
The sides AB, BC, CD, and DA touch the circle at points P, Q, R, and S respectively.

TO PROVE:
Parallelogram ABCD is a rhombus (i.e., AB = BC = CD = DA).

PROOF:
Step 1: Properties of parallelogram ABCD:
Since ABCD is a parallelogram, its opposite sides are equal in length:
AB = CD   ... (1)
AD = BC   ... (2)

Step 2: Circumscribed quadrilateral property (Theorem 10.2):
By Theorem 10.2, tangents from an external point to a circle are equal in length:
AP = AS, BP = BQ, CR = CQ, DR = DS.
Adding these four equalities (as established in Exercise 10.2 Q8):
(AP + BP) + (CR + DR) = (AS + DS) + (BQ + CQ)
AB + CD = AD + BC   ... (3)

Step 3: Substitute parallelogram properties (1) and (2) into (3):
Replace CD with AB, and BC with AD:
AB + AB = AD + AD
2 AB = 2 AD
Divide both sides by 2:
AB = AD   ... (4)

Step 4: Conclude all four sides are equal:
From (1), (2), and (4):
AB = BC = CD = DA.
Since all four sides of parallelogram ABCD are equal, ABCD is a rhombus.

Hence Proved!

[ROUGH_WORK]
Opposite sides equal (AB=CD, AD=BC). Tangent sums equal (AB+CD = AD+BC). 2(AB) = 2(AD) ⇒ AB = AD. Parallelogram with equal adjacent sides is a rhombus!
Boxed Answer: [ ABCD is a rhombus (Proved) ].

If the circumscribed parallelogram is a rectangle, what special geometric figure does it become?

worked_examples.given: ΔABC circumscribes a circle with centre O and radius r = 4 cm. D is point of contact on BC with BD = 8 cm, CD = 6 cm. E and F are contact points on AC and AB (Fig. 10.14).
worked_examples.formula: Theorem 10.2 (tangents from vertex are equal: BF = BD = 8, CE = CD = 6, AF = AE = x). Area of ΔABC = Area(ΔOBC) + Area(ΔOCA) + Area(ΔOAB) = r × s. Also Area(ΔABC) = √(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)) by Heron's formula.
worked_examples.substitution: Sides: a = 14, b = x + 6, c = x + 8. Semi-perimeter s = (14 + x + 6 + x + 8)/2 = x + 14. Area = r × s = 4(x + 14). Heron's Area = √((x+14)(x)(8)(6)) = √(48x(x+14)).
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Equate both area formulas:
   √(48x(x + 14)) = 4(x + 14)
2. Square both sides:
   48x(x + 14) = 16(x + 14)²
3. Since x + 14 ≠ 0, divide both sides by 16(x + 14):
   3x = x + 14 ⇒ 2x = 14 ⇒ x = 7 cm.
4. Calculate sides:
   AB = c = x + 8 = 7 + 8 = 15 cm.
   AC = b = x + 6 = 7 + 6 = 13 cm.
worked_examples.solution:
GIVEN:
ΔABC circumscribes a circle with centre O and radius r = 4 cm.
Point of contact on BC is D, with BD = 8 cm and DC = 6 cm.
Let the points of contact of the circle with sides AC and AB be E and F respectively (Fig. 10.14).

TO FIND:
Lengths of sides AB and AC.

STEP-BY-STEP CALCULATION:
Step 1: Apply Theorem 10.2 for tangent lengths from each vertex:
- From vertex B: BF = BD = 8 cm.
- From vertex C: CE = CD = 6 cm.
- From vertex A: Let AF = AE = x cm.

Step 2: Express the side lengths of ΔABC in terms of x:
- BC = a = BD + CD = 8 + 6 = 14 cm
- AC = b = AE + CE = x + 6 cm
- AB = c = AF + BF = x + 8 cm

Step 3: Calculate the semi-perimeter s of ΔABC:
s = (a + b + c) / 2
s = [14 + (x + 6) + (x + 8)] / 2 = (2x + 28) / 2 = x + 14 cm.

Step 4: Compute Area(ΔABC) by summing areas of ΔOBC, ΔOCA, and ΔOAB:
Join OA, OB, and OC. The perpendicular heights from in-centre O to sides BC, AC, and AB are all equal to the radius r = 4 cm:
Area(ΔOBC) = (1/2) × base × height = (1/2) × 14 × 4 = 28 cm²
Area(ΔOCA) = (1/2) × (x + 6) × 4 = 2(x + 6) = 2x + 12 cm²
Area(ΔOAB) = (1/2) × (x + 8) × 4 = 2(x + 8) = 2x + 16 cm²
Total Area(ΔABC) = 28 + (2x + 12) + (2x + 16) = 4x + 56 = 4(x + 14) cm²   ... (1)

Step 5: Compute Area(ΔABC) using Heron's Formula:
Notice:
s - a = (x + 14) - 14 = x
s - b = (x + 14) - (x + 6) = 8
s - c = (x + 14) - (x + 8) = 6
Area(ΔABC) = √(s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c))
Area(ΔABC) = √((x + 14)(x)(8)(6)) = √(48x(x + 14))   ... (2)

Step 6: Equate equations (1) and (2) and solve for x:
√(48x(x + 14)) = 4(x + 14)
Square both sides:
48x(x + 14) = 16(x + 14)²
Divide both sides by 16(x + 14) (since x > 0, x + 14 > 0):
3x = x + 14
3x - x = 14
2x = 14
x = 7 cm.

Step 7: Find side lengths AB and AC:
AB = x + 8 = 7 + 8 = 15 cm
AC = x + 6 = 7 + 6 = 13 cm.

[ROUGH_WORK]
Verification: s = 7 + 14 = 21. Area = r × s = 4 × 21 = 84 cm². By Heron's: √(21 × 7 × 8 × 6) = √(21 × 7 × 48) = √(147 × 48) = √7056 = 84 cm². Perfect match!
Boxed Answer: [ AB = 15 cm and AC = 13 cm ].

worked_examples.given: A quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle with centre O. Sides AB, BC, CD, and DA touch the circle at P, Q, R, and S respectively.
worked_examples.formula: SSS Congruence of constituent triangles and complete angle sum around a point = 360°.
worked_examples.substitution: Join OP, OQ, OR, OS and OA, OB, OC, OD. ΔOPA ≅ ΔOSA ⇒ ∠1 = ∠8. Similarly ∠2 = ∠3, ∠4 = ∠5, ∠6 = ∠7. 2(∠1 + ∠2 + ∠5 + ∠6) = 360° ⇒ ∠AOB + ∠COD = 180°.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Label the 8 angles at centre O formed by joining radii to points of contact: ∠AOP = ∠1, ∠BOP = ∠2, ∠BOQ = ∠3, ∠COQ = ∠4, ∠COR = ∠5, ∠DOR = ∠6, ∠DOS = ∠7, ∠AOS = ∠8.
2. In ΔOPA and ΔOSA: OP = OS (radii), AP = AS (tangents from A), OA = OA (common). By SSS congruence, ΔOPA ≅ ΔOSA. Thus ∠1 = ∠8.
3. Similarly: ∠2 = ∠3, ∠4 = ∠5, and ∠6 = ∠7.
4. Sum of all angles around point O is 360°:
   (∠1 + ∠8) + (∠2 + ∠3) + (∠4 + ∠5) + (∠6 + ∠7) = 360°
   2∠1 + 2∠2 + 2∠5 + 2∠6 = 360°
   2(∠1 + ∠2) + 2(∠5 + ∠6) = 360°
   2 ∠AOB + 2 ∠COD = 360° ⇒ ∠AOB + ∠COD = 180°.
5. Similarly, ∠BOC + ∠AOD = 180°.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: ∠AOB + ∠COD = 180° and ∠BOC + ∠AOD = 180° (Opposite sides subtend supplementary angles at centre)
worked_examples.solution:
STATEMENT:
Prove that opposite sides of a quadrilateral circumscribing a circle subtend supplementary angles at the centre of the circle.

GIVEN:
A quadrilateral ABCD circumscribes a circle with centre O.
The sides AB, BC, CD, and DA touch the circle at points of contact P, Q, R, and S respectively.

TO PROVE:
(i) ∠AOB + ∠COD = 180°
(ii) ∠BOC + ∠AOD = 180°.

CONSTRUCTION:
Join OP, OQ, OR, and OS (radii to points of contact).
Join the vertices to the centre: OA, OB, OC, and OD.

PROOF:
Step 1: Number the eight angles at centre O:
Let:
∠AOP = ∠1, ∠BOP = ∠2
∠BOQ = ∠3, ∠COQ = ∠4
∠COR = ∠5, ∠DOR = ∠6
∠DOS = ∠7, ∠AOS = ∠8.

Step 2: Prove pairwise angle equality using SSS congruence:
In ΔOAP and ΔOAS:
- OP = OS (Radii of the same circle)
- AP = AS (Tangents from external point A, Theorem 10.2)
- OA = OA (Common side)
By SSS congruence criterion:
ΔOAP ≅ ΔOAS.
Therefore, by CPCT:
∠1 = ∠8   ... (1)

By identical reasoning for pairs of triangles at vertices B, C, and D:
ΔOBP ≅ ΔOBQ ⇒ ∠2 = ∠3   ... (2)
ΔOCQ ≅ ΔOCR ⇒ ∠4 = ∠5   ... (3)
ΔODR ≅ ΔODS ⇒ ∠6 = ∠7   ... (4)

Step 3: Sum of all angles around point O:
The sum of all angles formed around the central point O is 360°:
∠1 + ∠2 + ∠3 + ∠4 + ∠5 + ∠6 + ∠7 + ∠8 = 360°

Step 4: Substitute from (1), (2), (3), (4) to group into opposite angles:
Replace ∠8 by ∠1, ∠3 by ∠2, ∠4 by ∠5, and ∠7 by ∠6:
∠1 + ∠2 + ∠2 + ∠5 + ∠5 + ∠6 + ∠6 + ∠1 = 360°
2(∠1 + ∠2) + 2(∠5 + ∠6) = 360°
2[(∠1 + ∠2) + (∠5 + ∠6)] = 360°
(∠1 + ∠2) + (∠5 + ∠6) = 180°.

From our angle definitions:
∠1 + ∠2 = ∠AOB (subtended by side AB)
∠5 + ∠6 = ∠COD (subtended by opposite side CD).
Therefore:
∠AOB + ∠COD = 180°.

Step 5: For the other pair of opposite sides:
Similarly, by grouping ∠2 + ∠3 + ∠6 + ∠7:
∠BOC + ∠AOD = 180°.

Conclusion:
Opposite sides of quadrilateral ABCD subtend supplementary angles at the centre O.
Hence Proved!

[ROUGH_WORK]
8 angles sum to 360°. Symmetry halves them: 2 × (∠AOB + ∠COD) = 360° ⇒ ∠AOB + ∠COD = 180°!
Boxed Answer: [ ∠AOB + ∠COD = 180° and ∠BOC + ∠AOD = 180° (Proved) ].
concept_questions: How does applying Theorem 10.2 at all four vertices lead directly to AB + CD = AD + BC?
Does every quadrilateral circumscribe a circle, or only those whose opposite sides have equal sums?
